lead: Two additive manufacturing families use a printhead. Material jetting fires droplets of liquid photopolymer or molten wax and cures them with ultraviolet light, like an inkjet printer. Binder jetting fires a liquid binder into a powder bed, gluing one cross-section at a time. Neither uses a laser or filament nozzle. They make smooth visual models, colour prototypes, wax casting patterns, and, in binder jetting, metal or foundry-sand parts finished in a furnace. The two mechanisms differ from SLS and SLA.
prereq: You need: AM classification in Chapter 7.1, photopolymer curing from Chapter 7.3, and the powder bed idea from Chapter 7.5.

sections.h3: Material jetting: droplets cured by UV light

blocks.text: A material jetting printer has a printhead with fine nozzles, like a home inkjet head. The head sweeps over the build platform and fires photopolymer droplets only where the slice needs material. A UV lamp beside the head travels the same track and cures the droplets at once, so one sweep leaves a solid line of plastic.

Layers are thin, usually 15 to 30 micrometres, because one droplet is a few tens of micrometres wide. Thin layers give smooth walls and sharp detail: a gear tooth or thin rib prints clean, with less stair-stepping than thick FDM layers.

Overhangs need support. The same head jets a soft gel where the part needs a scaffold. After the build the operator removes the part and washes the gel away with a water jet. A heated head can jet molten wax; that wax pattern goes into investment casting.

items: Slice the CAD model into layers 15 to 30 micrometres thick.
The platform starts empty; the head does the work.
Sweep the head along length L, firing droplets on slice pixels and gel on support pixels.
Pass the UV lamp over the same track to cure the layer.
Lower the platform one layer thickness and repeat.
Remove the part, wash away support gel, post-cure if needed.

blocks.text: Multi-jet modelling (MJM, also called PolyJet) is material jetting with many jets in one head. A block of nozzles covers a wide strip, so a full layer needs few sweeps. Two or more photopolymer resins load at once, and the slicing software chooses which jet fires at each point.

Mixing two resins in different ratios on one layer gives digital materials: a rigid resin blended with a rubber-like one gives intermediate stiffness in one part. Some machines add cyan, magenta, yellow and black resins, so a coloured model comes from one build.

MJM is not FDM. FDM melts a thermoplastic filament and drags it from a nozzle; MJM throws liquid droplets and cures them with light. MJM parts are photopolymer, so they are brittle, soften in strong sunlight and are not load-bearing.

blocks.where: t_total is print time in seconds; H is part height in mm; h is layer thickness in mm; W is part width across head travel in mm; w is printhead width in mm; L is sweep length in mm; v is print speed in mm/s. Powder spreading and head return are ignored; the same arithmetic applies to binder jetting.

sections.h3: Binder jetting: glue inside a powder bed

blocks.text: Binder jetting reverses the idea. The build box is filled with powder: polymer, ceramic, metal or foundry sand. A roller spreads a flat layer 0.08 to 0.2 mm deep. A printhead jets liquid binder, a glue, only on the cross-section pixels. The powder wets, the binder sets, and the layer bonds in the shape of the slice. The piston drops the bed one layer thickness, fresh powder spreads, and the cycle repeats.

At the end the box holds a cake of loose powder with the part buried inside. The operator digs it out and blows loose powder away. What remains is a green part: weak and chalky, like an unbaked sandcastle, held only by dried binder. Strength comes later. Options are oven curing, sintering in a furnace where the binder burns off and particles fuse, or infiltration with bronze or epoxy to fill pores. Sintering shrinks the part, so the CAD model is scaled up before printing.

items: No laser. Melting energy comes from a furnace outside the machine, so the printer is fast and cheap.
SLS melts powder with a laser, needs no binder, and gives a denser part in one machine.
SLA cures resin in a vat and uses no support powder.
Foundry sand is common: printed sand moulds and cores replace hand-rammed moulds and allow shapes patterns cannot make.

sections.h3: Which process, and where it is used

blocks.text: Pick material jetting or MJM when the surface must look right and the part is a visual aid: a coloured assembly model, a dental or medical model, a thin-walled prototype, or a wax pattern for investment casting. Pick binder jetting when the part is large, a furnace is available, or the product is a sand mould or core. Neither suits a part that carries load in service.

figure.caption: Jetting AM splits into two printhead families. Material jetting fires droplets that a UV lamp cures; binder jetting glues powder that a furnace later sinters or infiltrates.

spec.aria: A tree divides jetting AM into material jetting, with resin, wax and MJM, and binder jetting, with powder, binder and a cure or sinter step.

examples.question: A binder-jetted part is 25 mm tall, built with 0.1 mm layers. The layer to be printed is 100 mm wide across the head travel, the printhead is 10 mm wide, and the print speed is 200 mm/s. The sweep length equals the part width. Find the print time, ignoring powder spreading and head return.
steps: Number of layers = H / h = 25 mm / 0.1 mm = 250 layers.
Passes per layer = W / w = 100 mm / 10 mm = 10 passes.
Time for one sweep = L / v = 100 mm / 200 mm/s = 0.5 s.
Time per layer = passes × sweep time = 10 × 0.5 s = 5 s.
Total print time = layers × time per layer = 250 × 5 s = 1250 s.
examples.answer: The printhead needs 1250 s, that is 20.83 min (about 20.8 min), ignoring powder spreading.
examples.check:
H, h = 25.0, 0.1
W, w = 100.0, 10.0
L, v = 100.0, 200.0
layers = H / h
passes = W / w
t_pass = L / v
t_layer = passes * t_pass
t_total = layers * t_layer
print(layers)
print(passes)
print(t_pass)
print(t_layer)
print(t_total)
print(round(t_total / 60, 2))

traps: Binder jetting uses no laser. The binder glues powder; strength comes later from curing, sintering or infiltration. A laser sintering powder describes SLS.
The green part is not finished. It is weak, porous and shrinks during sintering, so the CAD model is printed oversize.
MJM is material jetting, not FDM. No filament or melting nozzle; resin is liquid and cured by UV.
Multi-jet modelling is not MultiJet Fusion, a powder-bed process with a similar name.
Print time formulas ignore powder spreading, depowdering, support removal and furnace time. Total lead time is longer.

quiz.q: What is the job of the UV lamp in material jetting?
quiz.a: It travels beside the printhead and cures fresh photopolymer droplets, so each sweep leaves a solid layer.

quiz.q: What holds a binder-jetted part together when it comes out of the powder bed?
quiz.a: Dried liquid binder between powder particles. This weak green part is later cured, sintered or infiltrated.

quiz.q: Why does MJM usually give a smoother surface than FDM?
quiz.a: MJM jets droplets and builds 15-30 micrometre layers; liquid wets the surface before curing. FDM extrudes filament, giving thicker layers, a visible raster and a nozzle-width track.

quiz.q: Why can an MJM machine print a part with graded stiffness, while SLA cannot?
quiz.a: MJM has several resin supplies and independent jets, so the slicer places different resins or mixtures at each point. SLA cures one vat, so the whole part is one material.

quiz.q: A binder-jetted part is 40 mm tall with 0.08 mm layers. The layer is 60 mm wide, the printhead is 12 mm wide and the print speed is 250 mm/s. Sweep length equals part width. Find the print time in seconds and minutes, ignoring powder spreading.
quiz.a: Layers = 40 / 0.08 = 500. Passes = 60 / 12 = 5. Sweep time = 60 / 250 = 0.24 s. Time per layer = 5 × 0.24 = 1.2 s. Total = 500 × 1.2 = 600 s = 10 min.

quiz.q: A metal bracket can be made by SLS-type powder bed fusion or by binder jetting plus sintering. Compare the two on bonding energy, part density and equipment.
quiz.a: Powder bed fusion supplies laser energy inside the machine to melt each slice, so no binder is present and the part is dense in one machine. Binder jetting supplies only glue; melting happens in a separate furnace after binder burn-out, so the part is porous until sintered or infiltrated, shrinks, and needs two machines. Binder jetting prints faster and cheaper per part and suits large parts and sand moulds.

quiz.q: A foundry wants a complex sand core with internal channels for a cast pump body. Explain why binder jetting suits this job better than machining the core from a sand block.
quiz.a: Binder jetting builds the core by gluing sand layer by layer from CAD, so internal channels and undercuts form without a pattern or split core box. Machining a sand block reaches only features open to the tool, and thin curved channels crumble. The printed core is cured and used directly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Metal binder jetting is used for production batches of small stainless-steel and copper parts, sintered in a batch furnace. Printed sand moulds and cores are common in Indian foundries making pump bodies, impellers and automotive castings, because no pattern is needed. Research pushes nanoparticle inks and jetted functional fluids, so conductive tracks and sensors can be printed inside a plastic part.
